title: Three times a day
hook: the Didache's rhythm: the Lord's Prayer morning, noon and night
tomorrow: what if reading less of the Bible is the point?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the morning offering, in set words or your own, and the line all of it. Now the day keeps moving, and it needs places to stop.

A stomach growls at midday, somewhere between one class or meeting and the next. In Acts, Peter's does too. He's staying in Joppa, in a house by the sea. Downstairs someone is getting a meal ready, and Acts says “he became very hungry.” Instead of hovering by the kitchen, he climbs to the flat roof: he “went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour.” Hot sun, the smell of cooking drifting up, and a set hour that took him upstairs.
screen: `A GROWL AT MIDDAY.` → `THE SMELL OF COOKING BELOW.` → `UP TO THE ROOF TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: Acts shows another set hour: “Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.” The first believers kept hours of prayer they already knew. And an early Christian handbook, the Didache, gives its own rhythm: pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day. It doesn't name the hours; it gives the prayer and the number. So why fixed times, when Paul says “Pray without ceasing”? Because a habit needs hooks. Three stops are how a day learns to pray always. Now the senses part. Set hours have often been carried by sound. In some churches a bell still rings at morning, noon and evening for a prayer called the Angelus. A bell, the height of the sun, the smell of a meal: the body knows the hour before the mind decides. Today an alarm can do the same work. And the sound comes on days nobody feels like praying, with the same short prayer waiting. Look at Peter's hour again: hungry, hot, dinner not ready. He prays anyway, and Acts says that's when the vision comes, a great sheet let down from heaven. An ordinary midday became the hour something new opened.
screen: `THE HOUR OF PRAYER, THE NINTH HOUR.` · `THE DIDACHE: THREE TIMES A DAY.` · `A SOUND THAT CALLS THE HOUR.` · `HUNGRY, AND PRAYING ANYWAY.` · then, large: `MORNING, NOON, NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Pick up your phone and set three quiet reminders: waking, midday, lying down. Choose one sound for all three, play it once now, and listen to it all the way to silence. If you pray, let that sound mean the Lord's Prayer; if not, let it mean one slow breath and a moment of attention.
Three times a day. The Didache's rhythm: the Lord's Prayer, said at set stops through the day.
Keep this: morning, noon, night, three stops and one short prayer. Until the next one.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray the Lord's Prayer or a short set prayer at fixed times each day, and some churches ring a bell at morning, noon and evening as a call to pray.
